subject: science

items.q: What is the Earth's core mainly made of?
items.correct: Iron and nickel metal
items.misconception: Molten rock called magma
items.why: Pupils see lava pour out of volcanoes and picture a molten centre feeding them. Capps, McAllister and Boone (2013, Journal of Geoscience Education) report studies in which 10–15-year-olds commonly believed the core was molten and the source of volcanic magma (Lillo, 1994), and 13–14-year-olds saw the core as the source of magma (Dal, 2007). The core is metal, mainly iron and nickel. Magma is melted rock that forms in small regions near the top of the mantle and in the crust.
items.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
items.random_wrong: The same rock as the crust

items.q: In the Earth's crust, how are most metals found?
items.correct: Joined to other elements in compounds
items.misconception: As lumps or veins of the pure metal
items.why: Pictures of gold nuggets and the phrase 'metal mining' suggest that metal is dug up ready-made, and pupils rarely see an ore. It is a common error teachers see. Most metals are found in compounds in rocks. A rock with enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting is an ore, and the metal has to be extracted from it.
items.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
items.random_wrong: Spread evenly through every kind of rock

items.q: By mass, iron is the most common element in the whole Earth, but oxygen is the most common in the crust. Which explains this?
items.correct: Most of the Earth's iron is in its core
items.misconception: Oxygen gas from the air soaks into rocks
items.why: Pupils meet oxygen as the gas we breathe and rarely think of it joined to other elements in solids such as sand (silicon dioxide). It is a common error teachers see. An element can be found as the element or joined in compounds. Most of the Earth's oxygen is in compounds in rocks, not in the air.
items.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
items.random_wrong: Most of the Earth's iron is in its mantle

items.q: Which statement about the Earth's crust is correct?
items.correct: It is a thin layer of solid rock
items.misconception: It is the thickest layer of the Earth
items.why: The ground beneath us seems endlessly deep, and diagrams often draw the crust far thicker than it really is. Capps, McAllister and Boone (2013, Journal of Geoscience Education) report that in Lillo's (1994) study of 10–15-year-olds, exaggerated thickness of the Earth's layers dominated the pupils' drawings. Compared with the whole Earth, the crust is as thin as the skin on an apple.
items.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
items.random_wrong: It floats on a layer of liquid magma

items.q: The diagram shows the Earth's layers, labelled P, Q, R and S. Which statement about layer R is correct?
items.correct: It is liquid iron and nickel
items.misconception: It is solid iron and nickel
items.why: Many simple diagrams show the core as one solid-looking ball, and pupils know that iron is solid at everyday temperatures. It is a common error teachers see. The core has two layers: a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.
items.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
items.random_wrong: It is liquid rock called magma

items.q: Lava pours out of a volcano. A pupil says this shows that the whole mantle is liquid. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Most of the mantle is solid rock
items.misconception: The mantle is a sea of liquid magma
items.why: Lava from volcanoes, and diagrams that colour the mantle red or orange, suggest that everything under the crust is molten. RSC Education's guide 'How to teach earth science at 11–14' calls the idea that the mantle is semi-liquid 'a persistent misconception across all age groups'. The mantle is mostly solid rock. Magma forms only where a small amount of rock melts, near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
items.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
items.random_wrong: The lava rises up from the Earth's core

items.q: How does sedimentary rock form?
items.correct: Layers of sediment are squashed and cemented
items.misconception: Wet mud and sand just dry out and harden
items.why: Pupils see mud dry hard in the sun, so drying seems enough to make rock. Kortz and Murray (2009, Journal of Geoscience Education) list 'Sedimentary rocks form by wet sediments drying' among college students' ideas; that younger pupils share it is our inference. Sediment must be buried, compacted and cemented to become sedimentary rock.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
items.random_wrong: Sediment melts near a volcano, then cools again

items.q: How does metamorphic rock form?
items.correct: Heat and pressure change rock without melting it
items.misconception: Rock melts deep underground, then cools again
items.why: Heat is part of how metamorphic rock forms, and pupils assume enough heat must melt the rock. Kortz and Murray (2009, Journal of Geoscience Education) list 'Metamorphic rocks melt' among college students' ideas; that younger pupils share it is our inference. Metamorphic rock forms without melting. Melting and cooling make igneous rock.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
items.random_wrong: Layers of sediment are pressed and cemented

items.q: The diagram shows water in a crack in a rock. The water freezes and thaws many times. What is this an example of?
items.correct: Physical weathering
items.misconception: Chemical weathering
items.why: Pupils learn that rainwater causes chemical weathering and carry this over to every process with water in it, including freeze–thaw. It is a common error teachers see. Decide by whether new substances form. Ice splitting rock is physical; acidic rain reacting with limestone is chemical.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
items.random_wrong: Erosion of the rock

items.q: Plant roots grow into cracks in a rock. As the roots grow, they split the rock apart. What is this?
items.correct: Biological weathering
items.misconception: Not a kind of weathering
items.why: The word 'weathering' sounds as if only the weather can do it. Dove (1997, International Journal of Science Education) found that 'many students regard weathering as solely related to atmospheric elements' in a survey of 16–19-year-olds; that younger pupils share it is our inference. Living things weather rock too: roots widen cracks and burrowing animals break rock up. This is biological weathering.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
items.random_wrong: Erosion of the rock

items.q: The diagram shows layers of rock near the top of a mountain. One layer contains fossil sea shells. What does this suggest?
items.correct: The layer formed from sediment on a sea bed
items.misconception: People carried the shells up the mountain
items.why: Pupils explain things by actions they know, and people do move stones. Bonaccorsi and colleagues (2019, Educational Journal of the University of Patras UNESCO Chair) found 7-year-olds suggesting that someone brought the rock from the sea up to the mountain, and Kortz and Murray (2009, Journal of Geoscience Education) list 'People play a role in moving sediments and rock' among college students' ideas. Fossils inside a rock were buried as the rock formed. Their surroundings tell you where the rock formed, even if it has since been moved by slow Earth movements.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
items.random_wrong: The shells were pushed up from the core

items.q: The diagram shows close-up drawings of granite and basalt. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Granite's magma cooled more slowly
items.misconception: Basalt's magma cooled more slowly
items.why: Pupils link cold with ice and frost forming quickly, so fast cooling seems to make bigger crystals. It is a common error teachers see. Crystals grow while the liquid is cooling. The longer this takes, the larger they grow: granite cooled slowly underground; basalt cooled quickly at the surface.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
items.random_wrong: Both are cemented grains of sediment

figure.alt: Two square close-up drawings side by side. The left square, labelled granite, is filled by 12 large crystals of different shades that fit tightly together. The right square, labelled basalt, is filled by about 150 tiny crystals that fit tightly together. A note below says both drawn at the same scale.

items.q: Coal and metal ores are called limited, or finite, resources. Why?
items.correct: They form far too slowly to be replaced
items.misconception: Only a few countries may mine them
items.why: In everyday language 'limited' often means restricted, as in 'limited edition' or 'limited access'. It is a common error teachers see. In science, a finite resource is one with a fixed total amount that we are using faster than it can be replaced.
items.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
items.random_wrong: There is only a small amount of each

items.q: Example figures for 1 kg of a metal: making it from ore uses 170 MJ (megajoules). Recycling scrap uses 4 MJ to collect it and 10 MJ to melt it. How much energy does recycling save?
items.correct: 156 MJ
items.misconception: 160 MJ
items.why:
Pupils picture the factory step and forget the collection rounds and transport. It is a common error teachers see. Energy used by recycling = energy to collect and sort + energy to reprocess.

Working: Energy used by recycling = 4 MJ (collecting) + 10 MJ (melting) = 14 MJ. Energy saved = 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ.
items.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
items.random_wrong: 166 MJ
items.working: Energy used by recycling = 4 MJ (collecting) + 10 MJ (melting) = 14 MJ. Energy saved = 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ.

items.q: Which of these is a renewable resource?
items.correct: Wood, because new trees can be planted
items.misconception: Aluminium, because cans can be recycled
items.why: Recycling and renewable resources are both described as making resources 'last', so pupils treat them as the same idea. It is a common error teachers see. Renewable means replaced naturally as fast as we use it. Recycling helps finite resources last longer but does not make them renewable.
items.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
items.random_wrong: Coal, because plants keep on growing

items.q: About what percentage of dry air is carbon dioxide?
items.correct: About 0.04%
items.misconception: About 21%
items.why:
Carbon dioxide is discussed so much, in lessons on breathing and in the news about climate, that pupils assume there is a lot of it. It is a common error teachers see. Carbon dioxide is a tiny part of the air, about 0.04%, but it still has an important effect on the Earth's temperature.

Working: Accepted composition of dry air: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.9%, carbon dioxide about 0.04% (about 420 parts per million in 2024).
items.specStatementText: the composition of  the atmosphere
items.random_wrong: About 4%
items.working: Accepted composition of dry air: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.9%, carbon dioxide about 0.04% (about 420 parts per million in 2024).

items.q: Dry air contains nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), argon (Ar) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). Which describes dry air?
items.correct: A mixture of elements and a compound
items.misconception: A mixture of compounds and an element
items.why: Pupils link 'compound' with 'more than one atom joined together'. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions) reports a class of 13–14-year-olds in which sulfur (S₈) was considered a compound 'due to the number of atoms in the molecule'. Count the types of atom, not the number of atoms: N₂ and O₂ are elements; CO₂ is a compound.
items.specStatementText: the composition of  the atmosphere
items.random_wrong: Nitrogen and oxygen joined together

items.q: Which statement about dry air is correct?
items.correct: Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths of it
items.misconception: Oxygen makes up about four-fifths of it
items.why: We breathe air to get oxygen, and 'fresh air' and 'oxygen' are used almost as if they mean the same thing. It is a common error teachers see. About four-fifths of dry air is nitrogen and about one-fifth is oxygen.
items.specStatementText: the composition of  the atmosphere
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide makes up about a fifth of it

items.q: How do greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, keep the Earth warmer?
items.correct: They absorb heat given off by the Earth
items.misconception: They let in more of the Sun's rays
items.why: Pupils think of warming as coming straight from the Sun and do not separate sunlight from the heat the Earth gives off. Boyes and Stanisstreet (2001, Canadian Journal of Environmental Education) report that 46% of Year 7 and 56% of Year 11 pupils thought global warming was caused by 'increased penetration of solar radiation'. Sunlight warms the surface; the surface gives off heat; greenhouse gases absorb some of that heat.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
items.random_wrong: They make a hole in the ozone layer

items.q: The graph shows carbon dioxide in the air, measured in Hawaii from 1960 to 2020. What is the main cause of this rise?
items.correct: Burning coal, oil and natural gas
items.misconception: More and more people breathing out
items.why: Pupils learn that we breathe out carbon dioxide and that there are more people than ever. It is a common error teachers see. Fossil fuels release carbon that was locked underground for millions of years; that is what adds extra carbon dioxide.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
items.random_wrong: The hole in the ozone layer

items.q: Large areas of rainforest are cut down and burned. Why does this add to global warming?
items.correct: Burning the wood adds carbon dioxide to the air
items.misconception: Less oxygen in the air makes the Earth warmer
items.why: Pupils learn early that trees 'make the oxygen we breathe', so oxygen is the first link they make between forests and the air. It is a common error teachers see. Link forests to carbon dioxide: trees take it in by photosynthesis, and burning or rotting wood releases it.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
items.random_wrong: It makes the hole in the ozone layer bigger

items.q: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the air. Can a rise in this small amount change the climate?
items.correct: Yes, as CO₂ absorbs heat from the Earth
items.misconception: No, as 0.04% is far too little to matter
items.why: Pupils judge importance by amount, and 0.04% sounds like nothing. It is a common error teachers see. What matters is what a gas does, not only how much there is: carbon dioxide absorbs heat, and nitrogen and oxygen do not.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
items.random_wrong: Yes, as it is a poison that pollutes the air

items.q: As the Earth's average temperature rises, which change do scientists expect?
items.correct: Sea level rises as ice melts
items.misconception: Sea level falls as seas evaporate
items.why: Pupils know that heat dries up puddles, so they expect warmer seas to shrink. It is a common error teachers see. Melting land ice and warmer, expanding seawater both raise sea level.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
items.random_wrong: Earthquakes become more common

items.q: Is the inside of the Earth the same all the way through?
items.correct: No. The Earth is layered: a thin rocky crust, a thick mantle of hot rock, a liquid metal outer core and a solid metal inner core.
items.misconception: The inside of the Earth is the same all the way through: solid rock like the crust, not separate layers.
items.why: We only ever see the rocks of the crust, so pupils extend them to the whole Earth. Capps, McAllister and Boone (2013, Journal of Geoscience Education) report that Sharp and colleagues (1995) found most 9–10-year-olds in the UK described the Earth's interior as solid and uniform; that some older pupils keep this idea is our inference. The Earth has layers that differ in what they are made of and whether they are solid or liquid: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.
items.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is the inside of the Earth filled with water?
items.correct: No. Below the crust are the mantle (hot, mostly solid rock) and the core (iron and nickel). There is no ocean of water filling the inside of the Earth.
items.misconception: The inside of the Earth is filled with water (or with water and magma).
items.why: Pupils know about underground water from wells and springs and imagine it filling the Earth. Capps, McAllister and Boone (2013, Journal of Geoscience Education) report a study of 13–14-year-olds (Dal, 2007) in which most thought the Earth was filled with either water or magma. Underground water is found only in the rocks of the crust. Deeper down are the solid rock of the mantle and the metal core.
items.specStatementText: the composition of the Earth
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Do magma and rocks come up from the Earth's core?
items.correct: No. The core is iron and nickel metal, far below. Magma forms where some rock melts near the top of the mantle or in the crust, and rocks form in or on the crust.
items.misconception: Magma, rocks and other materials in the crust come up from the Earth's core.
items.why: Pupils link the hot core with hot lava, so the core seems the obvious source. Kortz and Murray (2009, Journal of Geoscience Education) list 'Magma and rocks come from the core' among college students' ideas, and Capps, McAllister and Boone (2013) report that 10–15-year-olds in Lillo's (1994) study saw the centre of the Earth as the source of volcanic magma. The core's metal stays deep inside the Earth. Magma forms much nearer the surface, and sedimentary rock forms from sediment laid down at the surface.
items.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does it get colder deeper inside the Earth?
items.correct: No. The temperature rises with depth. The crust is the coolest layer and the inner core is the hottest.
items.misconception: It is colder deep inside the Earth, because the Sun's heat cannot reach it.
items.why: Caves and cellars feel cool, and pupils think of the Sun as the only source of heat. RSC Education's guide 'How to teach earth science at 11–14' reports the common belief that it is 'colder inside the Earth because the sun cannot reach it'. Rock gets hotter the deeper you go: deep mines are hot, and the inner core is thought to be over 5000 °C.
items.specStatementText: the structure of the Earth
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Do all rocks need the heat of a volcano, or melting, to form?
items.correct: No. Only igneous rock forms from molten rock. Sedimentary rock forms from sediment without melting, and metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting.
items.misconception: All rocks need the heat of a volcano, or melting, to form.
items.why: Volcanoes are the most dramatic rock-forming process pupils know, so heat seems necessary for any rock. Kortz and Murray (2009, Journal of Geoscience Education) list 'Volcanism is needed to provide the heat for rock formation' among college students' ideas; that younger pupils share it is our inference. Each rock type forms in its own way: igneous from cooling molten rock, sedimentary from compacted and cemented sediment, metamorphic from heat and pressure without melting.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks

items.q: Is pressing sediment into rock a metamorphic change?
items.correct: No. Compacting and cementing sediment makes sedimentary rock. Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure.
items.misconception: Any rock made by squashing is metamorphic, so pressing sediment into rock is metamorphism.
items.why: Both sedimentary and metamorphic rock are described with the word 'pressure', so pupils merge the two processes. It is a common error teachers see. Sediment squashed and cemented makes sedimentary rock; existing rock changed by heat and pressure makes metamorphic rock.
items.specStatementText: the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is any change to a rock a metamorphic change?
items.correct: No. Metamorphic change happens deep underground, where heat and pressure change an existing rock without melting it. Wearing rock away at the surface is weathering.
items.misconception: Any change to a rock, including weathering at the surface, is a metamorphic change.
items.why: 'Metamorphic' is often taught with the hook 'meta means changed', so pupils apply it to any change a rock goes through. It is a common error teachers see. Use 'metamorphic' only for changes made by heat and pressure deep underground. Changes at the surface, such as splitting and wearing away, are weathering and erosion.

items.q: Are weathering and erosion the same thing?
items.correct: No. Weathering breaks rock down where it is. Erosion wears it away and carries the pieces off, for example by rivers, wind or ice.
items.misconception: Weathering and erosion are the same thing: any breaking up of rock is erosion.
items.why: The two words are usually taught together ('weathering and erosion') and both wear rock away. It is a common error teachers see. Ask whether the pieces move. Breaking up in place is weathering; carrying the pieces away is erosion.

items.q: Is granite made of grains of sediment stuck together?
items.correct: No. Granite's crystals grew and locked together as magma cooled slowly underground, so granite is an igneous rock.
items.misconception: Granite and other crystal-filled rocks are made of grains of sediment stuck together.
items.why: The speckled grains in granite look like the grains in sandstone. Kortz and Murray (2009, Journal of Geoscience Education) list 'Granite is made from sediments' among college students' ideas; that younger pupils share it is our inference. Interlocking crystals show that a rock formed from cooling molten rock. Separate, rounded grains held together by cement show a sedimentary rock.

items.q: Does crystal size depend only on what the rock is made of?
items.correct: No. Two rocks made from similar magma can have very different crystal sizes, depending on how fast they cooled.
items.misconception: Crystal size depends only on what the rock is made of, not on how fast it cooled.
items.why: Pupils think of crystal size as a fixed property of a substance, like its colour. It is a common error teachers see. Crystal size records cooling: slow cooling gives large crystals, fast cooling gives small ones.

items.q: Does using, burning or rusting a material destroy its atoms?
items.correct: No. Atoms are never destroyed. Burning coal turns its carbon into carbon dioxide; rusting joins iron atoms to oxygen in rust; metals can be recycled.
items.misconception: Using a material destroys it: things that burn or rust are 'used up', and their atoms are gone. This is why resources run out.
items.why: Fuels seem to vanish when they burn, rusty iron crumbles, and everyday language says things are 'used up' or 'rust away'. It is a common error teachers see. Resources run out because they are not replaced, not because atoms are destroyed: the atoms end up in other substances or places.
items.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is a resource renewable if there is a lot of it?
items.correct: No. A resource is renewable only if it is replaced as fast as we use it. There may be a lot of a finite resource, but the amount is fixed.
items.misconception: A resource is renewable if there is a lot of it; 'finite' means there is only a small amount.
items.why: In everyday language 'running out' suggests there is not much left. It is a common error teachers see. Ask whether the resource is being replaced, not how much of it there is.
items.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does recycling mean using an object again as it is?
items.correct: No. Reusing means using an object again as it is. Recycling means reprocessing the material, for example melting it, to make new products.
items.misconception: Recycling means reusing an object as it is, with no reprocessing.
items.why: 'Reduce, reuse, recycle' are taught together, so recycling and reusing are easily confused. It is a common error teachers see. Recycled material has to be reprocessed, which uses energy; reused objects do not.
items.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does recycling use no energy?
items.correct: No. Collecting, sorting, transporting and reprocessing used materials all use energy, although usually less than making new material.
items.misconception: Recycling uses no energy at all.
items.why: Recycling is presented simply as 'good', and pupils do not see the lorries, sorting plants and furnaces involved. It is a common error teachers see. Count every step: collecting, sorting, transporting and reprocessing all use energy.
items.specStatementText: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling

items.q: Do coal, oil and ores form again fast enough to replace what we use?
items.correct: No. They formed over millions of years. They are forming far more slowly than we use them.
items.misconception: Coal, oil and ores keep forming fast enough to replace what we use (for example, because plants keep growing).
items.why: Pupils know coal comes from plants and that plants keep growing, but have little feel for millions of years. It is a common error teachers see. Fossil fuels and ores take millions of years to form, so on a human timescale they are not replaced.

items.q: Does the air around us contain about 4% carbon dioxide?
items.correct: No. About 4% is the carbon dioxide in air we breathe out. The air around us has about 0.04%, a hundred times less.
items.misconception: The air around us contains about 4% carbon dioxide.
items.why: Pupils remember from biology that breathed-out air contains about 4% carbon dioxide and apply the figure to all air. It is a common error teachers see. Breathed-out air has about 4% carbon dioxide; dry air has about 0.04%.
items.specStatementText: the composition of  the atmosphere
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is carbon dioxide the third most common gas in dry air?
items.correct: No. The third most common gas is argon, at about 0.9%. Carbon dioxide is about 0.04%.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the third most common gas in dry air, more common than argon.
items.why: Argon is rarely mentioned, while carbon dioxide is talked about all the time, so pupils rank it higher. It is a common error teachers see. In dry air: nitrogen about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.9%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%.
items.specStatementText: the composition of  the atmosphere

items.q: Is air a compound?
items.correct: No. The gases in air are not chemically joined to each other, so air is a mixture of elements and compounds.
items.misconception: Air is a compound, because it contains more than one type of atom.
items.why: Pupils often decide between element, compound and mixture by counting the types of atom present. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions) reports a class of 13–14-year-olds in which a mixture of two gases (krypton and neon) was judged a compound because there were 'two types of atom'. Look at whether the different atoms are joined. In air, nitrogen, oxygen and argon particles are separate, so air is a mixture.
items.specStatementText: the composition of  the atmosphere
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is clean air a pure substance?
items.correct: No. In science a pure substance contains only one substance. Even clean air contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide, so it is a mixture.
items.misconception: Clean air is a pure substance.
items.why: In everyday language 'pure' means clean or natural, as in 'pure mountain air'. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions) explains that 'to the learner any material may be considered a substance', and that air, unlike water or carbon dioxide, is not a pure substance to a chemist. Keep the everyday and scientific meanings apart: clean air is still a mixture of several substances.

items.q: Is the greenhouse effect caused by the hole in the ozone layer?
items.correct: No. They are different. The ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet light from the Sun; the ozone hole was caused by other gases (CFCs). The greenhouse effect is caused by gases such as carbon dioxide absorbing heat given off by the Earth.
items.misconception: The greenhouse effect is caused by, or is the same as, the hole in the ozone layer.
items.why: Both are invisible 'layers' high in the air, both are linked to the Sun's rays, and both are reported as damage to the environment. Boyes and Stanisstreet (2001, Canadian Journal of Environmental Education) found that 58% of Year 7 and 74% of Year 11 pupils in north-west England 'apparently fused ideas about global warming and ozone layer degradation'. Keep the two apart: ozone depletion lets in more ultraviolet light; greenhouse gases absorb heat given off by the Earth.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

items.q: Is global warming caused directly by the heat given out by burning?
items.correct: No. The heat given out by fires and engines is tiny compared with the effect of the extra carbon dioxide, which stays in the air for many years and absorbs heat given off by the Earth. Carbon dioxide itself does not burn.
items.misconception: Global warming is heat given out directly by burning: by fires, by hot exhaust gases, or by carbon dioxide itself 'burning' in the air.
items.why: Pupils feel the heat of fires and exhausts, and 'burning fossil fuels' and 'a hotter planet' are heard together, so the heat of burning seems to be the cause. It is a common error teachers see. The warming comes from the carbon dioxide that burning adds to the air, not from the heat of the flames.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is global warming part of pollution in general, such as litter?
items.correct: No. Global warming is caused mainly by extra greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide. Litter and dirty rivers are other problems; they are not its main cause or effect.
items.misconception: Global warming is part of pollution in general: litter, rubbish and poisonous or dirty air cause it, and it causes more pollution.
items.why: Pupils file all environmental problems under 'pollution'. Boyes and Stanisstreet (2001, Canadian Journal of Environmental Education) found pupils linking global warming with rubbish in rivers (44% in Year 7) and litter in the street (32% in Year 7), and Shepardson and colleagues (2011, Climatic Change) report students who believed that air pollution in general causes global warming. Ask which gases absorb heat given off by the Earth. Carbon dioxide does, even though it is not poisonous at the level in air.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is carbon dioxide a greenhouse gas?
items.correct: Yes. Carbon dioxide absorbs heat given off by the Earth. More of it in the air makes the Earth warmer.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is not a greenhouse gas; it does not absorb heat.
items.why: Pupils meet carbon dioxide mainly in breathing and photosynthesis, not as a gas that absorbs heat. Boyes and Stanisstreet (2001, Canadian Journal of Environmental Education) found that only 42% of Year 7 pupils knew that carbon dioxide adds to the greenhouse effect (68% in Year 11), and Shepardson and colleagues (2011, Climatic Change) note that 'most students do not consider carbon dioxide as a greenhouse gas' in the studies they review. Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are greenhouse gases: they absorb heat given off by the Earth.
items.specStatementText: the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

items.q: Will global warming cause more earthquakes?
items.correct: No. Earthquakes are caused mainly by movements of the Earth's tectonic plates. Scientists do not expect a warmer climate to make them more common around the world.
items.misconception: Global warming will cause more earthquakes.
items.why: Pupils group all natural disasters together. Boyes and Stanisstreet (2001, Canadian Journal of Environmental Education) found that 30% of Year 7 and 14% of Year 11 pupils thought an increase in the greenhouse effect would bring more earthquakes. Expected effects of warming include rising sea level, melting ice and more heatwaves; earthquakes come from plate movements.
